etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English alarme, alarom, borrowed from Middle French alarme, itself from Old Italian all'arme! (“to arms!, to the weapons!”), ultimately from Latin arma (“arms, weapons”).

definitions.definition: A summons to arms, as on the approach of an enemy.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Arming to answer in a night alarm.

definitions.definition: Any sound or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a warning sound to arouse attention; a warning of danger.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Joel 2:1:
quote.text: Sound an alarm in my holy mountain.
She went about the house in a state of real terror, and yet lied monstrously and wilfully, and invented many of the alarms she spread, and made many of the sounds we heard.

definitions.definition: A device intended to warn or give notice of approaching danger.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Lord Marshal, command our officers-at-armsBe ready to direct these home alarms.

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book I”, in [Elijah Fenton], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume I, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC, page III:
quote.text: Is it then true, as distant rumours run,that crowds of rivals for thy mother's charmsthy Palace fill with insults and alarms?

definitions.definition: Sudden surprise with fear or terror excited by apprehension of danger; in the military use, commonly, sudden apprehension of being attacked by surprise.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter I, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: Alarm and resentment spread through the camp.

definitions.definition: A mechanical device for awaking people, or rousing their attention.
An instance of an alarm ringing, beeping or clanging, to give a noise signal at a certain time.
(transitive) To call to arms for defense.
(transitive) To give (someone) notice of approaching danger or necessary action; to rouse to vigilance; to put on the alert.

quote.citation: 1838, Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu, Passage in the Secret History of an Irish Countess:
quote.text: When the carriage drew up in the grass-grown court yard before the hall-door, two lazy-looking men, whose appearance well accorded with that of the place which they tenanted, alarmed by the obstreperous barking of a great chained dog, ran out from some half-ruinous out-houses, and took charge of the horses;  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, of a device) To produce a warning of approaching danger or necessary action; to emit a signal intended to rouse a recipient to vigilance or put them on the alert.

quote.citation: 1985 March 21, National Transportation Safety Board, “2.2 Environmental Factors”, in Aircraft Accident Report: United Airlines Flight 663, Boeing 727-222, N7647U, Denver, Colorado, May 31, 1984‎[1], page 39:
quote.text: The tower cab supervisor and various pilots stated that the LLWAS system frequently alarms because of the thunderstorm activity present, and that airspeed losses are common as a result of convective wind shear.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To surprise with apprehension of danger; to fill with anxiety in regard to threatening evil; to excite with sudden fear.
(transitive) To keep in excitement; to disturb.
